Chapter One: The Everyday Reality of Running a Rural Bookshop
You know, there’s this real romance about owning a bookshop—especially one tucked away in a small Scottish town. People dream about quiet days surrounded by shelves, the soft sound of pages turning, and that lovely feeling when you match the perfect book to just the right reader.
But honestly? Life behind the counter is a lot more complicated. It’s full of unpredictable rhythms, little victories, and plenty of challenges—most of which never show up in anyone’s daydream about being a bookseller.
Picture this: Each morning in Wigtown starts with unlocking the shop’s heavy old door. The bell above it rings out, letting you know another unpredictable day is about to unfold. Inside, the shop is sprawling and just a bit chaotic—shelves are packed tight, almost groaning under the weight of thousands of second-hand books. There’s that familiar scent of old paper and dust in the air. Some folks find it comforting; others, well, not so much.
The first job every day is always the same. You’re sorting through yesterday’s leftovers—unsold books, scattered receipts, maybe even a forgotten umbrella tucked between the shelves.
Running a rural bookshop means you’re constantly switching hats. Sure, you’re keeping the place tidy and the till balanced, but there’s so much more going on. There's answering emails from people hoping to sell their old collections, negotiating with delivery drivers who are always in a hurry, and staying on top of endless paperwork. The phone rings off the hook. Sometimes, it’s a genuine inquiry; other times, the requests are so odd you just have to laugh. One caller might be searching for a rare edition that hasn’t been printed in decades. Another might ask about a book they vaguely remember from childhood—no title, no author, just a hazy memory.
The flow of the day changes as customers wander in, each bringing their own energy. Some are regulars—people you know by name, who stop in as much for a friendly chat as for the books themselves. Then there are tourists, drawn by the town’s reputation as Scotland’s National Book Town. You can spot them right away, eyes wide as they take in the endless shelves. Some folks browse quietly, happy to lose themselves among the stacks. Others want your full attention, firing off questions or sometimes complaints.
Not every encounter is a friendly one. You’ll meet customers who haggle over already modest prices, or treat you with impatience or even a bit of condescension. And then there are the people who bring in boxes of books to sell, hoping for a windfall, only to be disappointed when most aren’t worth much. Sorting through these collections? It’s tedious, and honestly, it rarely gets a thank you. But every so often, you stumble across a hidden gem—a first edition, a signed copy, or a book that seemed lost to time.
Even with all the challenges, there are moments that make it all worthwhile. Maybe it’s a child’s excitement at finding a favorite story, or an older visitor sharing memories of books from their youth. Sometimes, it’s just a quiet conversation about a beloved author. These little moments of connection—they’re what give the long hours and hard work real meaning.
Over time, the shop becomes more than just a business. It turns into a gathering place, a tiny refuge, and a vital part of the community.
So, running a rural bookshop isn’t for the faint of heart. The work is tough, the hours are long, and the financial rewards? They’re usually pretty modest. But if you love books, and you care about your community, there’s a real satisfaction in those daily rituals, the small wins, and knowing that, in your own way, you’re helping to keep the world of books alive.
